weeks.focus: Model and freeze the network path

evidence: Build review and Week 18 learning log
Evaluation, remediation, and Week 20 learning log

outcomes.statement: Model a client journey as a layered path with round-trip, byte, bandwidth-delay-product, and tail-latency budgets.
Trace DNS resolution, addressing, routing, caching, and discovery with explicit authority, expiry, and failure boundaries.
Relate TCP ordering, loss recovery, flow control, congestion control, and receiver behavior to measured goodput and tail latency.
Trace TLS authentication and handshake costs while preserving hostname, certificate, key, resumption, and trust boundaries.
Diagnose proxy, load-balancer, NAT, connection-pool, and slow-reader behavior with capacity, ownership, and cost evidence.
Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 through setup, multiplexing, stream isolation, fallback, observability, and client-network constraints.
Diagnose nine hidden network faults from preserved evidence before reveal and design reruns that separate credible causes.
Defend a protocol and topology decision through client outcomes, security, cost, ownership, migration, rollback, and reversal conditions.

resources.title: Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities
resources.purpose: Separate stub, recursive, authoritative, referral, and cache behavior.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2 and 4.3.2; draw the resolver actors and classify positive, referral, name-error, and temporary-failure outcomes.

resources.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
resources.purpose: Ground connection, ordering, retransmission, flow, and congestion claims in the current base specification.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2.2, 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8; map each mechanism to one lab observation and one unobserved kernel boundary.

resources.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
resources.purpose: Trace negotiation, authentication, key establishment, and resumption without weakening trust.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2, 4.1–4.4, and 9; annotate the lab handshake with authenticated identity, key ownership, and failure behavior.

resources.title: HTTP/2
resources.author_or_publisher: M. Thomson and C. Benfield; IETF
resources.purpose: Reason about streams, multiplexing, concurrency, flow control, and TCP-level blocking.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2, 5, and 8.2; predict which independent stream can and cannot progress after one packet loss.

resources.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
resources.author_or_publisher: J. Iyengar and M. Thomson; IETF
resources.purpose: Compare QUIC connection and stream recovery boundaries with TCP-carried multiplexing.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2, 6, 13, and 21; identify what the lab models, measures, and deliberately does not claim.

resources.title: The Road to QUIC
resources.purpose: Connect protocol mechanics to deployability, middleboxes, fallback, and operational learning.
resources.assignment: Read the complete article; record one deployment constraint, one measurement boundary, and one reversal signal for Transit Signal.

resources.title: Deploying and Debugging HTTP/3
resources.purpose: Study real deployment, load-balancing, firewall, and debugging failure modes.
resources.assignment: Watch the talk or use all slides with Lesson 8; write a fallback ladder and name the telemetry needed to operate it.
